name: Karakorum
info: Karakorum was a city of the Orkhon valley in central Mongolia, founded in 1220, the capital of the Mongol Empire from 1235 to 1260 and later of the Northern Yuan dynasty, and today a ruin beside the Erdene Zuu Monastery.

facts.founded: Genghis Khan rallied his troops at a place called Karakorum in 1218 and 1219, and the foundation of the city is usually said to have occurred in 1220. His successor Ögedei built city walls and a fixed palace from 1235.
facts.where: In the upper Orkhon Valley, in the north-western corner of the Övörkhangai Province of Mongolia, near the present town of Kharkhorin.
facts.known: Capital of the Mongol Empire from 1235 to 1260; the Palace of Myriad Peace; the Silver Tree of Guillaume Boucher; the account of William of Rubruck, who reached it in 1254; the great stupa temple; the Erdene Zuu Monastery built from its stones
facts.today: The ruins lie beside the Erdene Zuu Monastery in the upper part of the Orkhon Valley World Heritage Site, near the town of Kharkhorin.

t: Genghis Khan founded Karakorum in 1220 in a valley that earlier Xiongnu, Göktürk and Uyghur empires had used, and under Ögedei from 1235 it became a walled capital with a fixed palace.
It was the capital of the Mongol Empire until 1260, when the empire divided and Khubilai Khan made Dadu the seat of the Yuan dynasty, leaving Karakorum an administrative centre.
Ming armies occupied it in 1372 and 1380, and in 1585 its stones and bricks went into the Erdene Zuu Monastery; its site was identified in 1889.
dyk: A large tree of silver and other precious metals stood in the courtyard of the Khan's palace, with four golden serpents round the trunk and a mechanical angel that sounded a trumpet when drinks were wanted. It was designed by Guillaume Boucher, an enslaved Parisian goldsmith.
ev: The foundation of Karakorum is usually dated to this year
Ögedei Khan decrees the Palace of Myriad Peace and has city walls built
The Mongol Empire divides and Khubilai Khan develops Dadu as the capital of the Yuan Empire
Lingbei Province is founded and Karakorum remains the administrative centre north of the Gobi
A Ming army under Li Wenzhong occupies the city and causes severe damage
Abtai Sain Khan founds the Erdene Zuu Monastery on the palace site, using stones and bricks of Karakorum

sections.origins:
The Orkhon valley was a centre of the Xiongnu, Göktürk and Uyghur empires. To the Göktürks the nearby Khangai Mountains were the location of the Ötüken, the locus of power, and the Uyghur capital Karabalgasun stood 27 km north-west of where Karakorum was later built. The area is also considered one of the oldest farming areas in Mongolia.

In 1218 and 1219 Genghis Khan rallied his troops for the campaign against the Khwarazmian Empire at a place called Karakorum, but the foundation of a city is usually said to have occurred only in 1220. Until 1235 Karakorum seems to have been little more than a yurt town. The site had several advantages. It was more central to the growing empire, and the climate near the end of the Medieval Warm Period was warmer and moister than today, which gave abundant grass for grazing. The Orkhon flowed north to south in a region where most rivers run east to west, which eased travel by river and gave a point of control over the natural network. The place had also been the centre of power of earlier empires, and this expressed Mongol control over the largely non-Mongol population of the region. An older layer from the 8th century has been found under the 13th-century walls, and it has been theorised to be the Takhai Balgas mentioned in Mongolian chronicles.
sections.growth:
Only in 1235, after the defeat of the Jin empire, did Ögedei raise city walls and build a fixed palace. He decreed the Tumen Amgalan Ord, the Palace of Myriad Peace, in 1235, and it was finished in one year. The History of Yuan records its establishment in 1236. Twice a year the khan stayed in the city for an extended period, and Ögedei encouraged the elite of the empire to build houses near his palace in order to centralise his power over the empire.

Under Ögedei and his successors Karakorum became a major site for world politics. Möngke Khan had the palace enlarged and the great stupa temple completed. The Silver Tree was made for the centre of the city by Guillaume Boucher.

After 1260 the city declined in rank, but in 1299 it was expanded eastwards. In the first half of the 14th century a series of public buildings was erected, to which inscription stones bear witness, and the stupa temples were renewed in 1311 and again from 1342 to 1346. The first half of the 14th century was a new era of prosperity for the city.
sections.rulers:
Karakorum was the capital of the Mongol Empire between 1235 and 1260. Foreign rulers came to it: Russian princes usually went to Sarai, the seat of the Golden Horde, to have their right to the throne confirmed, but sometimes had to travel to Karakorum. After the death of Yaroslav Vsevolodovich in 1246, Batu Khan granted the patent for the throne of Vladimir to his brother Sviatoslav, but the conflict between Batu Khan and Güyük Khan led to competing appointments. Yaroslav's eldest sons Alexander and Andrey were summoned to Karakorum, where the grand princely throne was given to Andrey.

After the dissolution of the empire in 1260 into the Yuan Empire, the Ilkhanate, the Chaghatayid Khanate and the Golden Horde, Khubilai Khan developed Dadu, present-day Beijing, as the capital of the Yuan Empire. In 1271 Karakorum was reduced to an administrative centre of a provincial backwater of the Yuan dynasty. It kept a high ideological status as one of the camps of the Chinggisids, and after the foundation of Lingbei Province in 1307 it remained the administrative centre of the region north of the Gobi Desert.

After the collapse of the Yuan in 1368, Karakorum became the residence of Biligtü Khan in 1370, and the Northern Yuan used it as a capital. Batu-Möngke Dayan Khan made it a capital once again at the beginning of the 16th century.
sections.life:
William of Rubruck, a Flemish Franciscan missionary and papal envoy, left one of the most detailed accounts of the city, though not always a flattering one. He compared it unfavourably with the village of Saint-Denis near Paris and thought the royal abbey there ten times as magnificent as the Khan's palace. He also described the town as very cosmopolitan and religiously tolerant. The walled city had four gates facing the four directions, two quarters of fixed houses, one for the "Saracenes" and one for the "Cathai", twelve pagan temples, two mosques and a Nestorian church.

The palace was built in the Chinese architectural style, with three main buildings side by side. Rubruck described its hall as like a church, with a nave and two rows of pillars, the Silver Tree standing inside the middle door and the khan seated on a high place to the north. The non-palatial part of the settlement grew only to the north of the palace, in the manner of the traditional circular camp, which left the khan clear access to the river and the forested mountains to the south. Apart from the permanent palace there was a moving palace that settled in a ring on its stops. According to Juvayni, Ögedei invited people into the open yard of the treasure buildings and let them carry away all they could in a set time, and he gave frequent donations from the treasure to the city's poor.
sections.crises:
The division of the empire hurt the city. In the Toluid Civil War with Ariq Böke, Khubilai disrupted the town's grain supply in 1260. In 1277 Kaidu took Karakorum, and Yuan troops and Bayan of the Baarin ousted him the following year.

After the fall of the Yuan, Ming armies struck the city. In 1372 a Ming army under General Li Wenzhong occupied Karakorum and caused severe damage. In 1380 Ming troops occupied it again and later razed it. The permanent palace was destroyed by the Ming in 1388, although a moving palace remained in the region until 1585.

According to Saghang Sechen's Erdeni-yin Tobči, a kurultai decided in 1415 to rebuild the city, but no archaeological evidence of such a venture has been found. Karakorum was inhabited at the beginning of the 16th century, when Batu-Möngke Dayan Khan made it a capital again. In the following years the town changed hands between Oirads and Chinggisids several times and was then given up permanently.
sections.legacy:
In 1585 Abtai Sain Khan, the senior Genghisid of the central Mongolian region, restored the area of the permanent palace as a monastery, Erdene Zuu, using the stones and bricks of Karakorum. Fragments of the Sino-Mongolian inscription of 1342 are built into its walls. Erdene Zuu is likely the oldest surviving Buddhist monastery in Mongolia and became the mother monastery of Urga, present-day Ulaanbaatar, which Tusheet Khan Gombodorj founded in 1639.

The location of the city was long unclear. Its identification with Erdene Zuu was hinted at in the 18th century, and there was a dispute into the 20th century over whether the ruins of Karabalgasun were those of Karakorum. In 1889 Nikolai Yadrintsev conclusively identified the site as the Mongol capital, and Wilhelm Radloff confirmed his conclusion. The first excavations took place in 1933 and 1934 under D. Bukinich. Sergei Kiselyov concluded from his work of 1948 and 1949 that he had found Ögödei's palace, but the German-Mongolian excavations of 2000 to 2004 seem to identify the remains as the great stupa temple. The finds include paved roads, brick and adobe buildings, floor heating systems, the working of copper, gold, silver, iron and glass, four kilns, and ceramics and coins from China and Central Asia.

The ruins lie beside the present town of Kharkhorin in the upper part of the Orkhon Valley World Heritage Site. In 2023 the President of Mongolia announced a plan to rebuild the historical capital.

summary: Karakorum was founded in 1220 in the Orkhon valley and was the capital of the Mongol Empire from 1235 to 1260. After the empire divided it became a provincial centre, and Ming armies damaged it in 1372 and 1380. Its stones went into the Erdene Zuu Monastery.
notes: END: the article gives no year for the end of the city. The lead says it 'probably fell into dereliction at the start of the 15th century', yet the Decline section says it was inhabited at the start of the 16th century and made a capital again by Batu-Möngke Dayan Khan, then given up permanently after changing hands. I used end 1400 with endCirca true from the lead; the editor may prefer another value.

WALLS: the article says Ögedei erected city walls in 1235, but the palace section says the Yuanshi and the 1342 inscription state that he built a wall around the entire city in 1236. The palace decree is 1235 and the History of Yuan gives 1236 for its establishment; the palace section also says it was 'built in 1236'. I used 1235 for the decree and 1236 for the History of Yuan record.

MING: the Decline section says the Ming occupied the city in 1372 and 1380 and 'later razed' it; the Buildings section says the Ming destroyed the permanent palace in 1388. I gave 1388 only for the palace and left the razing undated.

CAPITAL DATES: the lead says capital 1235-1260; the Founding section mentions the foundation in 1220. The article's phrase 'capital of the Northern Yuan in the late 14th and 15th centuries' sits beside the claim of dereliction at the start of the 15th century; I wrote only that the Northern Yuan used it as a capital.
ADMINISTRATIVE CENTRE: the article gives 1271 for the reduction to an administrative centre but 1260 for the division; I kept both.

PALACE SITE: the article says the large building outside Erdene Zuu once thought to be the palace was actually the 90 m Pavilion of the Rising Yuan, and that Kiselyov's palace was later identified as the great stupa temple; the palace is now understood to lie under Erdene Zuu. I left out the pavilion. The dating 'built in 1236' and the 'finished in one year' after the 1235 decree are as given.

ABTAI SAIN KHAN: the article gives 1585 for the restoration of the palace area as a monastery; I did not date the founding of Erdene Zuu otherwise. 'Likely the oldest surviving Buddhist monastery in Mongolia' is the article's hedge.
Left out: the Yelü Chucai poem, the Ring of the Avars, the Virtual Kharakhorin project of 2020, the ger-district of Ulaanbaatar and the details of the khuree comparison with Urga, as digressions.
Rubruck's date: the article says he reached Karakorum in 1254 and elsewhere that he entered it in April 1254 with the Khan's moving palace after four months; I used 1254 only.
The article gives no population figure for the city.
